learningObjectives.title: Public health and the fight against disease

questions.q: Who wrote the influential 1842 'Report on the Sanitary Conditions of the Labouring Population of Great Britain'?
questions.explain: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report linked poverty, dirt and disease and pressed for government action on sanitation.

questions.q: In which year was Britain's first Public Health Act passed?
questions.explain: The first Public Health Act of 1848 set up a General Board of Health but its powers were weak.

questions.q: Why did the 1848 Public Health Act have only a limited impact?
options: Its measures were permissive rather than compulsory
It banned local councils from building sewers
It was repealed within a year
questions.explain: Because towns were not forced to act, many councils avoided the cost and public health improved slowly.

questions.q: Who proposed the Germ Theory of disease in 1861?
questions.explain: Louis Pasteur's Germ Theory argued that microbes in the air, not spontaneous generation, caused decay and disease.

questions.q: Which disease-causing microbe did Robert Koch identify in 1882?
questions.explain: Koch identified the bacterium causing tuberculosis in 1882, having pioneered methods to stain and grow microbes.

questions.q: Why is John Snow's 1854 investigation of the Broad Street pump seen as significant?
options: It provided strong evidence that cholera spread through contaminated water, before Germ Theory was accepted
It proved that cholera was caused by bad air (miasma)
It led directly to the discovery of penicillin
It showed that cholera could not be prevented
questions.explain: By mapping deaths around the pump, Snow linked cholera to dirty water even though the microbe had not yet been identified.

questions.q: Why was the 1875 Public Health Act more effective than the 1848 Act?
options: It made many public health measures compulsory for local authorities
questions.explain: The 1875 Act forced councils to provide clean water, drainage and sanitation, unlike the voluntary 1848 Act.

questions.q: Which disease did Paul Ehrlich's 'magic bullet' Salvarsan 606 (1909) treat?
questions.explain: Salvarsan 606 was the first chemical 'magic bullet', developed by Ehrlich's team to target the microbe causing syphilis.

questions.q: What was meant by a 'magic bullet' in early twentieth-century medicine?
options: A chemical that destroyed a specific disease-causing microbe without harming the body
A vaccine made from weakened viruses
A surgical instrument for removing tumours
questions.explain: A magic bullet was a synthetic chemical designed to seek out and kill one particular microbe, such as Salvarsan or Prontosil.

questions.q: What was the key contribution of Howard Florey and Ernst Chain to the story of penicillin?
options: They purified and mass-produced penicillin so it could be used as a treatment
They first observed penicillin killing bacteria in 1928
They invented the antiseptic carbolic spray
questions.explain: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, but Florey and Chain developed methods in the 1940s to produce it in useful quantities.

questions.q: A town in the 1850s suffers repeated cholera outbreaks. Using John Snow's findings, which action would most reduce deaths?
options: Providing a clean, separate supply of drinking water
Encouraging people to keep their windows shut against bad air
Moving the cemeteries out of the town
Burning tar to clear the atmosphere
questions.explain: Snow showed cholera spread through contaminated water, so a clean supply removed the route of infection.

questions.q: A scientist wants to prove which specific microbe causes a particular disease. Whose methods would guide this work?
options: Robert Koch's techniques for staining and culturing bacteria
questions.explain: Koch developed the methods of growing microbes on cultures and staining them so individual disease-causing bacteria could be identified.

questions.q: Which anaesthetic did James Simpson discover the effects of in 1847?
questions.explain: James Simpson discovered that chloroform could safely anaesthetise patients, and it was soon widely used in surgery and childbirth.

questions.q: Which anaesthetic did the American dentist William Morton demonstrate in 1846?
questions.explain: Morton publicly demonstrated ether as an anaesthetic in 1846, though it was an irritant and could be dangerous.

questions.q: Why did surgical death rates sometimes rise in the years just after anaesthetics were introduced (the 'black period' of surgery)?
options: Pain-free patients allowed surgeons to attempt longer, deeper operations, which increased infection and bleeding
Anaesthetics themselves were the main cause of infection
questions.explain: With pain removed, surgeons operated more ambitiously before antiseptics existed, so infection and blood loss killed more patients.

questions.q: Which substance did Joseph Lister use as an antiseptic from 1865?
questions.explain: Lister used carbolic acid on wounds, instruments and in a spray to kill germs and reduce deadly post-operative infection.

questions.q: Which scientific idea inspired Joseph Lister to develop antiseptic surgery?
options: The theory of the four humours
The miasma theory of bad air
questions.explain: Lister reasoned that if germs in the air caused decay, killing them with carbolic acid would prevent wounds from becoming infected.

questions.q: What did Karl Landsteiner discover in 1901 that later helped make blood transfusions safer?
options: The existence of different blood groups
questions.explain: Landsteiner's discovery of blood groups meant donors and patients could be matched, preventing fatal transfusion reactions.

questions.q: A surgeon in 1870 wants to lower the number of patients dying from infection after operations. Following Lister, what should he do?
options: Use carbolic acid to kill germs on wounds and instruments
Operate more quickly and avoid washing at all
Give patients larger doses of chloroform
Keep the operating theatre completely dark
questions.explain: Lister's antiseptic method used carbolic acid to destroy germs, sharply reducing deaths from post-operative infection.

questions.q: On which date did the National Health Service (NHS) begin?
questions.explain: The NHS was launched on 5 July 1948, providing healthcare free at the point of use for all.

questions.q: The 1942 Beveridge Report identified 'five giants' to be defeated. Which set correctly names them?
options: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness
War, Poverty, Crime, Hunger and Fear
Want, Debt, Illness, Dirt and Cold
Disease, Famine, Death, War and Sin
questions.explain: Beveridge's five giants of Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness shaped the post-war welfare state, including the NHS.

questions.q: In 1948 a low-paid worker falls ill but has no money for a doctor. How does the newly created NHS change his situation?
options: He can receive medical treatment free at the point of use
He must pay the doctor before being seen
He can only be treated by a charity hospital
He must join a private insurance scheme first
questions.explain: The NHS, led by Health Minister Aneurin Bevan, provided care funded by taxation and free at the point of use for everyone.
